vignette:
He is 38, a Middle Eastern man who has spent most of his adult life standing behind a salon chair, his hands moving with easy confidence through other people's hair. He is known by clients as warm, meticulous, and calm, someone who remembers how a person likes their fringe to fall and what was happening in their life the last time they came in. Before he became ill, he works long days and likes the rhythm of the salon: the hum of dryers, the smell of product, the small intimacy of touch and conversation. He lives alone, is close to a few cousins, and keeps much of his own private life contained.

The illness begins with what he first dismisses as exhaustion. He tells himself he is just overworked. Then there is the fever, the dizziness, the shortness of breath that comes on suddenly while he is cutting a client's hair. He remembers gripping the counter and trying not to alarm anyone, insisting he just needs water. Within days he is in the hospital, and what he expects to be a brief stay turns frightening very quickly. He speaks of that period in flashes rather than a full story: harsh lights, machines sounding at odd hours, the feeling that his body no longer belongs to him. At one point, a doctor explains that his condition is serious and that they need to monitor him closely because things can worsen fast. What stays with him is not the exact medical language but the unmistakable sense that he might die.

He remembers lying awake through the night, listening for footsteps in the corridor, trying to read the faces of staff as they enter the room. Every shift change feels dangerous. If someone looks serious, his chest tightens. He starts watching the monitor compulsively, as though by staring at the numbers he can keep himself alive. He is ashamed now when he describes how terrified he is. He says he has never felt so helpless, not even as a child. He cannot get up without assistance. He cannot breathe normally. He cannot reassure the people calling him because he does not believe his own reassurances. In the worst moments he thinks, very plainly, I am not leaving here.

He survives, and other people treat that fact as the end of the story. For him, it is not. When he returns home, his body is weaker, but what unsettles him more is how impossible it is to feel safe again. At first he tells himself he just needs rest. Instead, he begins waking abruptly at night with the same jolt of fear he felt in the hospital, heart pounding, convinced for a few seconds that he cannot breathe. Sometimes he dreams he is back in the bed with tubes attached, trying to call out while no one comes. Other nights he does not sleep much at all because he is monitoring every sensation in his chest and throat.

During the day he becomes preoccupied with signs of illness. A minor cough, a little fatigue, a moment of lightheadedness can unravel him. He checks his temperature repeatedly. He searches online for symptoms, then hates himself for doing it. If he passes the hospital on the way to work, he looks away. The antiseptic smell in a pharmacy can make him suddenly feel cold and unsteady. On bad days he hears an ambulance siren and is right back in that room, his stomach dropping before he even understands why.

At the salon, the effects show in ways his clients do not always see. He still comes in dressed carefully, still tries to be attentive, but he is not as effortless as he once is. If the shop gets too warm, he panics that he is becoming feverish. If he has to climb stairs quickly or stand for too many back-to-back appointments, he becomes acutely aware of his breathing. He excuses himself to the bathroom to splash water on his face and check whether his lips look pale. A client casually mentioning a relative's hospitalization can leave him distracted for the rest of the appointment, his smile fixed, his mind pulled elsewhere. He has started shortening his schedule, telling coworkers he wants "better balance," though privately he fears being trapped at work while his body fails again.

His world has narrowed in small, humiliating ways. He avoids making plans too far ahead because he does not trust his health. He keeps medications, water, and a phone charger arranged neatly beside his bed, as if preparing for an emergency every night. Friends invite him out, and he often declines, saying he is tired. The truth is that restaurants feel risky, crowded places feel hard to escape, and being far from help makes him uneasy. He feels older than 38. He feels betrayed by his body and misunderstood by people who tell him he should be grateful and move on.

What he returns to in conversation is the loneliness of having almost died in a way other people cannot see. There are no scars that make sense to others. In the mirror he still looks like himself: stylish, put together, capable. But inside, ordinary sensations can still become evidence of catastrophe. He misses the version of himself who trusted tomorrow without thinking about it. Even now, months later, when he opens the salon in the morning and the dryers begin to hum, there are moments he feels almost normal. Then a tightness in his chest or the memory of hospital light crosses his mind, and the fear rises again, immediate and familiar, as though the danger has only briefly stepped out of the room.
